approved: Appropriation Bill (No. 2) 2021–2022 seeks $20 billion from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for non-ordinary annual services, including $12.7 billion for Defence, over $3.5 billion for infrastructure, $600 million for agriculture and environment (with $500 million for plantation development loans), and $400 million for the Local Roads and Community Infrastructure Program, with a revised Advance to the Finance Minister of $3 billion.

The bill proposes total appropriations of $287.5 million for four parliamentary departments in 2021-22. The largest allocation, $226.2 million, goes to the Department of Parliamentary Services for maintenance of Parliament House and support functions.

Three appropriation bills for 2021-2022—Appropriation Bill (No. 1), Appropriation Bill (No. 2), and Appropriation (Parliamentary Departments) Bill (No. 1)—were referred to the Federation Chamber for further consideration upon adjournment of the second reading debate.

The speaker supported the appropriation bills, arguing the budget prioritises vaccination and economic recovery while delivering record federal funding to Western Australia, including $13.2 billion in total payments, $5.3 billion in GST, $1.6 billion for infrastructure, and $2.8 billion for health.

The speech argued that the Morrison government's budget fails the electorate of Calwell and offers no substantive policy, contrasting it with Labor's proposed $100 million for 10,000 new energy apprenticeships and up to $10,000 per apprentice, as well as plans to criminalise wage theft. It also criticised the government's aged care response, highlighting $1.35 million in annual wage theft and a $3.2 billion supplement to providers without accountability.

The speaker argued that the federal government has failed to provide clear direction on COVID-19, including vaccination timelines, while shifting blame to state governments and creating confusion. They also called for bringing electric vehicle manufacturing to Australia, citing the US as an example, and noted that Australia's vaccination rate remains in the single digits compared to 50% in the US.

The speaker argued that the government's budget bills reflect lazy and inept economic management, having run up $1 trillion in debt—$40,000 per person—with no meaningful reform or public benefit, and that debt was doubled before the COVID-19 pandemic.
